data.kind: Results (bloods 6 days ago; pelvic ultrasound 3 days ago)
values: Left adnexa: 74 × 61 × 58 mm complex, predominantly solid-cystic mass; thick irregular septations, papillary projections, marked internal vascularity on colour Doppler
Uterus normal size; endometrium normal; right ovary normal; moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
Features highly suspicious for ovarian malignancy. Urgent gynaecological oncology referral recommended; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging

script.opening: “Hiya — sorry about the background, I’m on the boat. I’ve come to get my results. The nurse thought it was a fibroid — is that what it is?”

facts.text: “I’m inside the boat on my own. Dev’s outside doing the ropes.” If asked whether she wants him: “Yeah… can he come in?” Dev joins and sits quietly.
Bloating and swelling “like I’m pregnant” for about six weeks. Full after a few mouthfuls. Weeing more often. Tired.
“My jeans are tight on the belly but my face and arms have got thinner — about 5 kilos down.” Breathless going up the lock flights the last couple of weeks; fine at rest; no chest pain, no cough.
Periods regular, last one 2 weeks ago. No bleeding between periods or after sex. No discharge. Bowels a bit constipated. Not pregnant — “we’re careful, Dev’s had the snip”.
“I was adopted — I don’t know anything about my birth family.”
When the doctor mentions cancer or a growth that could be cancer: go silent, then cry for about a minute. Then: “But I’m only 43.”

facts.topic: Moving today (say when the doctor talks about referral or appointments)
facts.text: “We have to move the boat today. We’ve overstayed — we’ve had a letter. We’re heading north, but I don’t know where we’ll end up.” Post goes to a friend’s house in town. “The signal on the canal is rubbish.”
Works casual shifts at a canal-side café. Does not smoke, drinks little. Dev, 46, does boat maintenance. Registered at the practice 8 months ago while moored locally.

Start cheerful and practical. Ask for Dev if offered. Cry when cancer is mentioned and take a minute. Mention the move when referral is discussed. If the doctor says to wait until you are settled, accept it (this is a fail). If the doctor offers to refer today and works out contacts with you, become calmer and agree. Ask: “Will they be able to find me?” and “Is it going to kill me?”

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the boat must move today after an enforcement notice; she does not know where they will stop, post goes to a friend and phone signal is poor, so she fears she will “fall through the cracks”. Once told, she fears dying young.
ice.expectations: An explanation of the results and, she assumes, a routine gynaecology referral.

cues: “It’s the fibroid, isn’t it?” — she is not expecting bad news.
“The signal on the canal is rubbish.” — contact will be difficult.
“We have to move the boat today.” — the referral must not wait.

checkpoints.text: Checks identity, privacy and whether she wants her partner present before giving results; establishes what she already knows

Asks about relevant symptoms (weight loss, early satiety, urinary and bowel change, breathlessness, PV bleeding) and family history, and interprets the CA-125 and ultrasound together (RMI well above 250)
Gives a warning shot, breaks the news clearly that the results are very suspicious of ovarian cancer, allows silence and responds to her distress
Refers today on the suspected cancer pathway to gynaecological oncology and explains next steps (CT, specialist clinic, MDT, likely surgery)

Addresses the move: does not delay the referral; records the best phone numbers and email, confirms consent to contact Dev, explains registration anywhere without a fixed address and redirection of the referral, and suggests asking to stay within reach on health grounds
Provides copies of results, a named contact and a call within 48 hours; safety-nets for worsening breathlessness, abdominal pain or swelling, vomiting or bowel obstruction
Answers “Is it going to kill me?” honestly without false reassurance or catastrophising, and checks what she will take away

worked.txt: “Before we look at the results — are you somewhere you can talk privately? Would you like Dev with you?”
“The results aren’t what we hoped. The scan didn’t show a fibroid.”
“It showed a growth on your left ovary, and with the blood test, I’m worried it is very likely to be an ovarian cancer. I’m so sorry.” — then silence.
“I’m not going to wait until you’re settled — I’ll send the urgent referral today. Let’s make sure they can always reach you.”

“I can’t tell you yet how serious it is — that depends on whether it has spread, which the scan and specialists will find out. Many people are treated with surgery and chemotherapy, and the team will talk you through everything.”

f.learning: Results that strongly suggest cancer must be acted on the same day, whatever the logistics: a suspected cancer pathway referral can be made now and redirected later; waiting for a patient to “settle” is a serious error. For an adnexal mass, NICE recommends calculating the Risk of Malignancy Index (U × M × CA-125); an RMI of 250 or more warrants specialist gynaecological oncology MDT care, and an ultrasound suggestive of ovarian cancer meets the NG12 criteria for a suspected cancer pathway referral. Breaking bad news by video needs the same structure as face to face (SPIKES: setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, emotions, strategy) plus checks on privacy and connection. People without a fixed address — boaters, Gypsies and Travellers, people who are homeless — are entitled to register with any GP practice without proof of address. Protect continuity with multiple contact routes, written copies of results, a named contact and a booked follow-up call.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, updated 2026) · NICE CG122 Ovarian cancer: recognition and initial management (2011, updated 2026) · NHS England Patient registration — standard operating principles for primary medical care (2023) · GMC Good medical practice (2024)
knowledge.summary: Break bad news well, refer today on the suspected cancer pathway, and build the contact plan around a patient who has to move on.

points.t: CA-125 486 with a complex solid-cystic mass, papillary projections, vascularity and free fluid. RMI = U (3: multilocular, solid areas, ascites) × M (1: premenopausal) × CA-125 (486) ≈ 1458. Raised CRP and platelets fit malignancy; CA-125 can also rise with endometriosis, fibroids, menstruation and inflammation, but not to this picture.

Suspected cancer pathway referral to gynaecology (oncology) today; attach the results. The specialist team arranges CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, MDT discussion and usually surgery with or without chemotherapy. Breathlessness may be a pleural effusion — ask and safety-net.

Check identity, privacy, connection and who is present; ask what she knows; warning shot; clear words (“cancer”); silence; acknowledge emotion; then a plan. Offer a further call — people retain little after bad news.

A practice cannot refuse registration for lack of a permanent address; the practice address or a care-of address can be used. The patient can register as a temporary resident wherever they are. e-RS referrals can be redirected; the receiving team needs reliable phone numbers.

Record two or three phone numbers and an email, with consent to contact the partner; share results via the NHS App or printed copy; a named clinician or care navigator; a follow-up call in 48 hours; tell her to call if no appointment arrives within a week.
Adopted — unknown family history. All women with non-mucinous epithelial ovarian cancer are offered germline BRCA testing by the specialist team.

model.text: Hello Tamsin, it’s Dr Chen. Before we go through the results — can you see and hear me OK, and are you somewhere private? Would you like Dev to join you?
Yes — can he come in? … OK. It’s the fibroid, isn’t it?
Before I explain, can I check how you’ve been? Any weight loss, feeling full quickly, change in your waterworks or bowels, or breathlessness?
model.why: Completes the clinical picture and gauges understanding

model.text: Lost about 5 kilos, full after a few mouthfuls, weeing more, a bit puffed on the locks.

Thank you. I’m afraid the results aren’t what we hoped. The scan didn’t show a fibroid. It showed a growth on your left ovary, and with the blood test, I’m worried it is very likely to be an ovarian cancer. I’m so sorry.
(pause) This is a huge shock. Take your time — I’m here.

What needs to happen next is an urgent appointment with a specialist cancer team for ovaries. I’m going to send that referral today. They’ll do a CT scan and plan treatment, which is often an operation.
We have to move the boat today — we’ve had a letter. I don’t know where we’ll stop. Will they be able to find me?

I’ll make sure they can. I’ll send it today, not wait. Let’s take your number, Dev’s — with your permission — and an email. You can register with a GP anywhere you moor, even without an address, and the referral can be moved. Could you ask the Canal & River Trust about staying nearby for health reasons? And I’ll send the results to your NHS App.
model.why: Continuity plan for a mobile patient

model.text: Is it going to kill me?
I can’t answer that yet — it depends on whether it has spread, and the scan will tell us. Many people are treated successfully, and the team will be honest with you at every step.
model.why: Honest, neither false reassurance nor catastrophising

model.text: I’ll ring you in two days to check the appointment and how you’re both doing. If you get more breathless, severe tummy pain, keep vomiting or can’t open your bowels, call 111 or go to A&E. What will you tell Dev you’re both doing next?
Wait for the hospital call, keep the phone charged, ask about staying nearby, and you’ll ring Thursday.

social.t: Continuous cruisers must move regularly; patchy signal and care-of post make appointments easy to miss. Plan multiple contact routes.
Dev’s presence helps retention and practical planning; confirm consent to share information with him.

legal.t: Practices should not refuse registration because a patient cannot provide proof of address or has no fixed address.
Record her consent for the hospital and practice to contact Dev.

professional.t: An abnormal result with a radiologist recommending urgent referral must be acted on the same day and the action documented.

community.t: Target Ovarian Cancer and Ovacome; Macmillan; boater welfare officers (Canal & River Trust); local cancer navigator.

redFlags: Leg swelling (VTE risk with pelvic mass)
ice: Concern: falling through the cracks; dying young
core: Weight, satiety, urinary and bowel change

playbook.diagnosis: Complex left adnexal mass with markedly raised CA-125 and free fluid — highly suspicious of ovarian cancer (RMI about 1458).
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A growth on your left ovary that is very likely to be a cancer — the specialists need to confirm it and plan treatment.”

management.reflectIce: “You came expecting a fibroid, and you’re worried you’ll be lost in the system while you move. I’ll send the referral today and make sure they can reach you.”
management.psychosocial: Dev involved; boater welfare support; cancer charities; café work and money.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to gynaecological oncology today
Contacts: her number, Dev’s (consent), email; NHS App results
Register with a GP wherever they moor; referral can be redirected
Ask about staying within reach on health grounds
Call in 48 hours; named practice contact
safetyNet: Breathlessness, severe abdominal pain, vomiting or no bowel opening — 111 or A&E
Call the practice if no hospital contact within a week

pitfalls.intro: Strong communication can still fail this station if the referral waits for her to settle.

items.fail: “Call me when you know where you’ll be and I’ll refer you there.”
items.why: Delays a suspected cancer referral by days or weeks.
items.fix: Refer today; redirect later if needed.

items.fail: Delivers the news straight away without checking privacy or support.
items.why: She is on a boat with her partner outside; bad news needs a prepared setting.
items.fix: Check privacy and offer Dev first.

items.fail: Reads out the CA-125 and scan without asking about breathlessness or weight.
items.why: Misses possible effusion and the full picture.

timeMap.d: What she knows; symptoms; family history.
Warning shot, clear words, silence, empathy.
Referral today; contacts; registration anywhere; staying within reach.

wordPics.clearFail: Tells her it is “probably a fibroid but we’ll refer”, or breaks the news bluntly with no setting; delays referral until she settles.
wordPics.fail: Breaks the news reasonably but does not refer today, or refers without any plan for contact while she moves.
wordPics.pass: Sets up the conversation, breaks the news clearly with empathy, refers on the suspected cancer pathway today, explains next steps, builds a contact plan and arranges follow-up.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus: uses silence well, involves Dev with consent, answers the prognosis question honestly, uses practical solutions for a boater (registration anywhere, NHS App, staying within reach) and confirms understanding.

avoid.instead: “I’m worried it is very likely to be an ovarian cancer.”
avoid.why: False reassurance destroys trust when the diagnosis is confirmed.

avoid.dont: “Let me know when you’ve settled and I’ll send the referral there.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll send it today and make sure they can reach you wherever you are.”
avoid.why: Suspected cancer referrals must not wait.

avoid.instead: “I can’t say yet how serious it is — the scan will tell us more.”
avoid.why: Honest uncertainty is kinder than promises.
